concepts.topicTitle: Human Biological Evolution and Dispersal Out of Africa
concepts.label: Studying Early Human History: Evolution and Writing
concepts.cardText: The period before the development of writing is understood mainly through archaeological evidence. More than 99 per cent of human history falls before writing (from about 3 million years ago to 5000 years ago), and less than 1 per cent in the last 5000 years. Before writing, tools and other material objects (artefacts) are the major sources; after it, both material remains and written documents are sources, and dating becomes relatively more accurate because documents mention specific dates. Early human history helps us understand humankind's biological and cultural evolution in relation to climate and environment. Biological evolution is the gradual physical and genetic change through which australopithecines evolved into modern Homo sapiens; cultural evolution explains how humans adapted to their surroundings during the Quaternary Period, developing tools and technology and moving from hunting and gathering to agriculture. Surplus food and goods laid the foundation for civilisation.

concepts.topicTitle: Human Biological Evolution and Dispersal Out of Africa
concepts.label: Human Ancestors and Their Dispersal Out of Africa
concepts.cardText: Our earliest ancestors evolved and lived in Africa and began to move out around 2 million years ago. Homo erectus, an early human ancestor with stone tools such as hand axes and cleavers, was the first hominin to exit Africa. Another major wave of movement out of Africa took place around 125,000 years ago with the early Homo sapiens, modern humans, who evolved in Africa about 300,000 years ago. Archaeologists explore sites for tools, bones and other objects, and experiment by making similar tools. Around 3.3 million years ago one human ancestor made the earliest stone tools, marking the beginning of 'human behaviour', and humans came to be known as hominins, or tool makers, whose tools were extra-corporal limbs. Fossils are preserved remains that turn to stone. Homo habilis lived in Africa, especially the Olduvai Gorge; Homo erectus invented handaxes and cleavers and migrated; Homo sapiens developed complex technologies.

concepts.label: The Ages of Early Human History and the Palaeolithic Hunter-Gatherers
concepts.cardText: Early human history is divided into distinct periods based on technological progress: the development and use of tools, the beginning of agriculture, and changes in lifestyle and settlement. The Stone Age is broadly divided into the Palaeolithic, Mesolithic and Neolithic stages. Palaeo means 'old' and lithic means 'stone', so the Palaeolithic is the Old Stone Age, a hunting-gathering lifestyle with simple stone tools. In the Indian subcontinent the oldest human settlement dates back about 2 million years ago, with Attirampakkam in Tamil Nadu dated to 1.5–1.7 million years ago and Isampur in Karnataka to 1.2 million years ago, where handaxes and cleavers, scrapers and choppers were found, used to chop meat, dig tubers, scrape skin and cleave bones for marrow. Later smaller tools such as scrapers, borers and points, then the bow and arrow, microblade tools, cave paintings, pigments and beads appeared, with symbolic communication.

concepts.label: Mesolithic Hunter-Gatherers
concepts.cardText: Around 12000 years ago the Earth's climate became warmer, leading to significant changes: forests and grasslands expanded into areas previously covered by ice sheets, and the new landscapes offered more resources, including small game animals, fish and edible wild grains. The world witnessed the first-ever population explosion in human history. A variety of microlithic tools enabled people to gather aquatic food, marine and freshwater, and fishing was the mainstay of their subsistence economy. Art flourished and new habitats such as caves and rock shelters were frequently occupied; the World Heritage Site of Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh has hundreds of painted rock shelters with Mesolithic and earlier occupation. The Mesolithic is a transitional phase between hunting-gathering and agriculture using tiny stone (microlithic) tools.

concepts.topicTitle: The Neolithic Revolution and Agricultural Village Life
concepts.label: The Neolithic Revolution
concepts.cardText: As hunter-gatherers gained familiarity with seasons and different types of food resources, there was a gradual transition to a food-producing way of life, known as the Neolithic revolution. Its hallmark was the domestication of select animals and plants, bringing them under human control, and the development of new breeds through cultivation and husbandry. While hunter-gatherers made tools for procuring food, Neolithic farmers made tools for food production and processing and developed earthenware pottery in many shapes and sizes. They established the first village settlements, laying the foundations for the urban revolution. The transition did not occur at the same time everywhere but at different periods in different areas, such as wheat and barley in West Asia, millets and rice in India and China.

concepts.topicTitle: The Neolithic Revolution and Agricultural Village Life
concepts.label: The Neolithic in the Indian Subcontinent: Mehrgarh
concepts.cardText: In the Indian subcontinent there was regional variation in the start of agriculture. In the north-west, the site of Mehrgarh on the Bolan River, in present-day Pakistan, is the oldest Neolithic site and the earliest agricultural village, dating to about 7000 BCE. Its people built handmade sun-dried brick houses and granaries, buried their dead in graves and made ornaments from semi-precious stones like lapis lazuli, carnelian and shells. They cultivated wheat and barley and raised sheep, goats and Indian cattle, in particular the zebu humped bull. They were also the first to make copper objects, becoming known as the Chalcolithic people by about 4000 BCE, which laid the basis for the Bronze Age Sindhu–Sarasvatī civilisation around 3500 BCE. By 2500 BCE most of the subcontinent was occupied by Neolithic agricultural communities.

concepts.topicTitle: Emergence of Metal Age Culture and the Early Harappan Transition
concepts.label: The Early Harappan Stage of the Sindhu–Sarasvatī Civilisation
concepts.cardText: Some settlements in the Mehrgarh culture mastered the extraction of copper from its ores around 4000 BCE and became the earliest Chalcolithic sites in the subcontinent, marking the beginning of the Bronze Age. The introduction of copper tools in the fertile alluvial plains of the Indus and the Ghaggar-Sarasvatī basins enhanced productivity and prosperity, with large-scale pottery showing regional styles. Since these sites show cultural continuity, this stage is described as Early Harappan, with continuity in pottery, semi-precious stone beads, shell bangles, terracotta and copper working. Perimeter walls around settlements, the use of seals and even the script probably began in this stage. Graffiti on pottery and seals with geometric and animal motifs were forerunners of the script and seals. The Early Harappans ploughed fields at Kalibangan with double-crop furrows, and used standard weights, binary multiples for small units and tens for larger. Technological advances and economic integration led to the emergence of urban centres.

concepts.topicTitle: Comparative Bronze Age Civilisations of the Ancient World
concepts.label: River-Valley Civilisations and the Mesopotamian Civilisation
concepts.cardText: Four early world civilisations emerged in river plains: the Harappan along the Sindhu and Sarasvatī rivers, the Mesopotamian around the Euphrates and Tigris, the Egyptian along the Nile, and the Chinese in the Huang He basin. Mesopotamia, 'the land in between', was the earliest city-based civilisation, and its closeness to the Indus region helped strong trade contacts with the Harappans. The four major city-based civilisations from 3500 BCE were the Sumerian, Akkadian, Assyrian and Babylonian. The Sumerians were the first to build dams and canals for irrigation and to use mud and burnt bricks, built a ziggurat for each city's chief god, and the temple authority tied together farming, trade and transport. They were first to write, around 3200 BCE, in cuneiform, pressed with wedge-shaped reeds on clay tablets. The Akkadians under Sargon set up the first dynastic empire and traded with Meluhha, identified with the Sindhu–Sarasvatī civilisation; Hammurabi of Babylonia compiled the Code of Hammurabi.

concepts.topicTitle: Comparative Bronze Age Civilisations of the Ancient World
concepts.label: The Egyptian Civilisation
concepts.cardText: The Egyptian civilisation is one of the earliest civilisations, known for its rich historical records. Egyptian history is reconstructed from papyrus records, made by cutting the inner trunk of the papyrus plant into strips, pressing and drying them into sheets. The Rosetta Stone, found in 1799 with three types of writing including Greek, helped Jean-François Champollion decipher the script in 1822. City-states emerged around 3000 BCE; the Nile flooded every summer, leaving rich black mud, 'kemet', excellent for crops. About 5000 years ago farmers dug ditches to divert Nile water into fields and stored water, and counting days between floods produced a calendar. The collective effort led to local government. Powerful pharaohs emerged as rulers, buried beneath mastabas which were stacked to form pyramids because the Egyptians believed each person had a ka, a spiritual double that lived on if the body was preserved through mummification. Egyptian society was a hierarchy from pharaoh to serfs and slaves, and women could own property and run businesses.

concepts.topicTitle: Comparative Bronze Age Civilisations of the Ancient World
concepts.label: The Chinese Civilisation
concepts.cardText: The Chinese civilisation flourished along the Huang He (Yellow River) and the Yangtze, centres of early Chinese Neolithic cultures dating to around 7000 BCE. Around 2000 BCE copper/bronze metallurgy brought many Neolithic settlements to the threshold of the Bronze Age, and around 1600 BCE urban centres began to emerge with greater agricultural productivity and advances in metallurgy and crafts, giving rise to the first Chinese Bronze Age territorial empire, under dynasties such as the Shang and Zhou. By 600 BCE iron was widely used; the name 'China' probably comes from the Qin dynasty, the first imperial dynasty, followed by the Han. The earliest source about China is the 'oracles', symbols on animal bones and tortoise shells heated until they cracked. The script is logographic. Jade objects, bronze vessels, silk (a major trade item on the 'Silk Route' from the Han) and the Great Wall are notable; China first introduced paper currency and civil services through public examination.
